h1: Tourism Business Website Guide: Homestays, Resorts, and Restaurants

inline: a practical guide for tourism businesses — homestays, guesthouses, resorts, and restaurants — on what a website actually needs to do, how booking systems work, what photography costs, and how to reduce OTA dependency. It is written for owners, not developers.

Tourism businesses have different website requirements than any other kind of business. The website has to sell an experience (not a product), handle bookings (not just inquiries), and support seasonal demand (not year-round demand). This guide covers what is specific to tourism, and how to build a website that actually gets bookings.

inline: A tourism website is not a product website and not a brochure site. It is a sales tool for an experience, and it has to do specific things that other kinds of websites do not.

b: You are selling an experience, not a product.

items: A product has a spec sheet. An experience has photos, atmosphere, reviews, and location. The website has to convey all of that in a way a product page does not.
A tourism business needs the website to convert visitors into confirmed bookings, not just phone calls or emails. That requires a booking flow, not just a contact form.
Tourism businesses live by seasonal patterns. The website has to handle seasonal pricing, seasonal availability, and seasonal content — all of which are updatable without a developer.
A restaurant can get away with mediocre photos if the food is good. A homestay cannot — the photos are what the guest is buying. Good photography is not optional.
Travelers rely heavily on reviews. The website has to display reviews, link to Google reviews, and build trust signals.
Most tourism searches happen on mobile, often at the last minute. A site that works poorly on mobile loses bookings.

blocks.text: What a tourism website does not need

items: — you are selling a stay, not a product. A booking flow is different from a cart and checkout.
— guests do not need to log in; they need to book quickly.
— unless you have a specific content strategy, a blog is a distraction from the booking flow.
— unless you have a significant international guest base, English plus Hindi/Marathi is usually enough.

inline: The booking system is the most important decision in a tourism website. It determines how guests book, how much you pay in fees, and how much control you have over the guest relationship. The four options below are the main ones, with their trade-offs.

head: Option
Cost
Fees
Best for
rows: Homestays with 1–3 rooms and low inquiry volume
Businesses that already use OTAs and want to add direct bookings
Very small homestays with low booking volume, or businesses just starting out

inline: The simplest and cheapest option. The guest fills in a form with their dates and contact details, and the form sends a WhatsApp message or email to you. You reply manually to confirm availability and take payment.
zero cost, no monthly subscription, personal communication.
manual confirmation, slower response, guests may abandon if they want instant confirmation.

A real booking engine that shows real-time availability, calculates rates, and processes payment. Typically built on a hospitality booking platform (Staah, AxisRooms, or similar) that integrates with the website.
instant confirmation, real-time availability, professional experience, reduces staff time.
higher upfront cost, monthly subscription, more complex to set up and maintain.

The booking engine integrates with OTAs (Booking.com, MakeMyTrip, Airbnb) so that availability is synced across all channels. A guest can book directly on your website, and the booking is reflected in your OTA calendars.
same as Option 2, plus guaranteed availability sync across channels. No double bookings.
higher cost, more complex setup, requires coordination with OTA account management.
The website shows the property, describes the rooms, and links to the OTA listings for booking. The guest books on the OTA, and you pay the OTA commission.
lowest website cost, familiar booking experience for guests.
OTA commission on every booking, no direct guest relationship, no control over the listing.

blocks.text: Which option is right for you

items: Option 1 (booking form) is usually sufficient.
Option 2 or 3 (booking engine) is usually worth it.
Option 3 (booking engine + OTA sync) is usually necessary.

b: Very small homestay with low volume:

items: Option 4 (OTA links) may be sufficient, but it does not solve the commission problem.

inline: For a tourism business, photography is not a nice-to-have — it is the product. A guest choosing a homestay or resort is choosing based on the photos more than any other factor. Poor photos cost bookings regardless of how nice the property actually is.

blocks.text: What good tourism photography looks like

items: Photos taken during golden hour or with bright natural light, not harsh flash or dim indoor lighting.
Every room from multiple angles, the exterior from multiple angles, the view from the property.
Photos that show the size of the rooms and the property — a wide shot of the room, not just a close-up of the bed.
Close-ups of the small things that make the property special — the breakfast, the garden, the view from the balcony.
Some tourism photos include people to show scale and atmosphere; others do not. Either is fine, but it should be consistent.
Photos in the same lighting and style across all rooms and areas.
A stock photo of a beach that is not your beach is misleading and will be spotted.
Phone cameras are good in daylight; in dim indoor lighting they are not.
Mixed lighting and styles across a gallery looks unprofessional.

b: Photos that are clearly from a different season.

items: A photo of a sunny beach in a listing for a monsoon stay is misleading.
₹15,000 to ₹50,000, depending on the photographer, the property size, and how many rooms are being shot.
₹10,000 to ₹30,000 extra, worth it for resorts with distinctive geography.

b: Copy photo editing from your own photos:

items: ₹2,000 to ₹10,000, if you have good raw photos but need them edited.

blocks.text: When photography is worth the investment

inline: For a homestay, guesthouse, or resort, professional photography is almost always worth it. The cost is small relative to the booking revenue it can generate. A ₹20,000 photography investment that increases bookings by even 10% pays back within a season. For a small restaurant or activity provider, professional photography is also worth it, but the scope can be smaller — a half-day shoot rather than a full property shoot.

blocks.text: How to use the photos on the website

items: — the single best photo, above the fold.

b: Gallery on every room or service page

items: — 3–6 photos per room or service.
— photos next to each room option in the booking form.
— Open Graph images that show the property when the page is shared.

inline: Most tourism businesses get a significant portion of their bookings through OTAs — Booking.com, MakeMyTrip, Goibibo, Airbnb, and similar platforms. OTAs are a legitimate way to get bookings, but they come with costs and limitations that a direct booking channel avoids.

items: On a ₹3,000 weekend night, the OTA takes ₹450 to ₹750.
The OTA owns the guest's contact information. You cannot market directly to them after the stay.
The OTA controls the listing page. You cannot fully control the story that is told.
You compete with every other property for top placement, and OTA ranking algorithms favor paid placements and high review counts.
Only payment gateway fees (2–3%) if you take online payment, or nothing if the guest pays on arrival.
You own the contact information and can market directly for future stays.
The website is entirely yours — photos, copy, pricing, positioning.
Guests who book direct are much more likely to book direct again. A repeat guest list is a real asset.

inline: Most tourism businesses should not abandon OTAs — they are a valuable source of new guests, especially at the start. The right mix is usually: OTAs for discovery and new guests, the website for direct bookings from returning guests and referrals. As your direct booking channel grows, the OTA share can decrease, but it rarely goes to zero, and that is fine.

blocks.text: How to grow the direct channel

b: A website with a clear booking flow.

items: The essential first step.
When guests search for a homestay or restaurant in your area, your listing should be prominent.
Google reviews influence both the Google Business Profile and the website's trust.
Collect WhatsApp numbers from direct guests and send periodic offers for off-season stays.
A 10–15% discount for returning guests is a strong incentive and cheaper than OTA commission.

b: A "book direct" message on the website.

items: Tell guests why booking direct is better for them — often a better rate, more flexibility, direct communication.

inline: Tourism businesses live by seasonal patterns. The website has to handle seasonal pricing and availability without requiring a developer for every update.

items: Friday and Saturday nights are usually priced higher than weeknights.
Diwali, New Year, school holidays, and festival periods are priced higher.
Monsoon and low-season periods are priced lower, sometimes with additional offers.
Sometimes lower, to fill empty rooms on short notice.

blocks.text: How to display seasonal pricing on the website

items: A calendar showing rates for each date, updated in the admin panel.
A card per room type showing the rate range (e.g., "₹2,500 weekdays, ₹3,500 weekends").
A banner at the top of the site announcing the current season's rates or offers.
A discount code or offer visible only on the website, not on OTAs.

blocks.text: How to make seasonal pricing updatable

inline: The website should be built on a platform that lets you update pricing yourself — without calling the developer. For a simple site, this might be a WordPress admin panel. For a booking engine site, it might be the booking platform's rate management interface. Either way, the ability to update pricing without a developer is essential for a seasonal business.

blocks.text: What to ask a developer about seasonal pricing

items: Can I update pricing and availability myself, without calling you?
How do I set different rates for weekends, holidays, and off-season?
Can I display a rate calendar, or do I have to update rates manually on each room page?
Can I create seasonal offers that are visible only on the website, not on OTAs?

inline: Pricing is only part of seasonal content. A tourism website should also be able to show:

items: — the property in monsoon, in summer, in winter.
— what is available during the current season (e.g., water sports in summer, birdwatching in winter).
— restaurants, activities, and other services may have seasonal hours.
— "Book early for Diwali weekend" or "Monsoon specials available now."

inline: Travelers rely heavily on reviews when choosing where to stay or eat. Reviews are a major factor in both search ranking and booking conversion, and a tourism website has to make reviews prominent.

items: — the most important, because they show up in Google search and on Google Maps.
— Booking.com, MakeMyTrip, Airbnb reviews, which potential guests will check independently.
— especially for restaurants and activities.
— quotes collected from past guests, published on the website.

blocks.text: How to display reviews on the website

items: — a selection of reviews from various sources, with links to the source.

b: Reviews on room or service pages

items: — 2–3 reviews per room type or service, relevant to that specific offering.
— a live widget showing the current Google reviews and rating.
— a summary at the top of the site (e.g., "4.8 from 120 Google reviews").
A simple "Please leave a Google review" card at checkout or in the room.

b: Ask via WhatsApp after the stay.

items: A follow-up message a day after checkout, with a direct link to the Google review page.
Responding to reviews signals to Google and to future guests that you engage with feedback.
A direct link to the Google review page, not a multi-step process.
Acknowledge the issue, say what you are doing about it, and invite the guest to return.
A defensive response looks worse than the negative review itself.

b: Fix the problem if it is real.

items: A negative review about a fixable issue is an opportunity, not a defeat.
Hiding negative reviews is worse than the reviews themselves — future guests will find them elsewhere.

inline: A tourism website needs a specific set of pages and features. The list below covers the minimum for a homestay, guesthouse, resort, or restaurant.

items: — the hero photo, a short pitch, the location, and a clear "Book" or "Check availability" button.
— one page per room type, menu section, or activity, with photos, description, and pricing.
— a selection of the best photos of the property, rooms, and surroundings.
— where you are, how to get there, and a map.
— a selection of reviews and a link to your Google reviews.
— the story of the place and the people.
— phone, WhatsApp, email, and a contact form or booking form.
— either a booking form or a booking engine page, linked from every page.
— the primary conversion mechanism; every page should have a clear path to it.
— prominently displayed, especially on mobile.
— the site should be designed for mobile first, then adapted for desktop.
— under 3 seconds on 4G for the first load.
— Google Business Profile, local schema, and local keyword targeting.
— showing seasonal pricing, updatable by the owner.
— showing current Google reviews and rating.
— for businesses with steady demand.
— if you have international guests.
— a page with nearby attractions, restaurants, and activities, which is useful for guests and good for SEO.
— photos grouped by season.
— a discount or offer visible only on the website.
— unless you have a specific content strategy, a blog is a distraction.
— 300–500 words is enough; guests do not read long stories.
— guests do not need to log in; they need to book quickly.
— a mobile-friendly website is sufficient for most tourism businesses.

faqs.q: What does a tourism business need on its website?
a: A homepage, room or service pages with photos, a gallery, a location page, a reviews section, an about page, and a contact page — plus a booking flow (form or engine), a WhatsApp button, mobile-first design, and local SEO. See the

faqs.q: Do I need a booking engine or is a booking form enough?
a: For a homestay with 1–3 rooms and a low volume of inquiries, a booking form via WhatsApp is sufficient. For a guesthouse or resort with 4+ rooms and steady demand, a booking engine is usually worth the investment. See the

faqs.q: How do I reduce my dependency on OTAs?
a: Build a direct booking channel: a website with a clear booking flow, an optimized Google Business Profile, a strong review strategy, and a repeat-guest program. OTAs are still valuable for discovery, but a strong direct channel reduces your commission costs over time. See the

faqs.q: How do I handle seasonal pricing on my website?
a: Use a content management system or booking platform that lets you update pricing yourself, without a developer. Set different rates for weekends, holidays, and off-season, and display them clearly on the site. See the

faqs.q: Should I hire a local developer or a remote one for a tourism website?
a: For most tourism websites, a remote developer is fine. Local matters if you need in-person photography, a developer who can visit the property, or emergency support during peak season. See the

faqs.q: How important are reviews for a tourism website?
a: Very important. Travelers rely heavily on reviews when choosing where to stay or eat, and reviews are a major factor in both search ranking and booking conversion. The website should display reviews prominently and link to Google reviews. See the

faqs.q: Do I need a blog on my tourism website?
a: Usually not. A blog is a distraction from the booking flow unless you have a specific content strategy. A well-built brochure-and-booking site is more valuable than a mediocre blog. See the

faqs.q: How long does it take to build a tourism website?
a: A homestay site with a booking form takes 4 to 6 weeks. A guesthouse with a booking engine takes 6 to 8 weeks. A resort with OTA integration takes 8 to 12 weeks. The timeline depends on the complexity and how quickly you provide content and feedback.

faqs.q: Can I integrate my website with my existing OTA listings?
